sections.html:
New Jersey has five municipalities named Washington Township, plus Washington Borough in Warren County. This page covers Washington Township in Gloucester County, the South Jersey community of Sewell, Turnersville and Grenloch with about 49,840 residents. Check the county on your tax bill if you are not sure which one you live in.

If your house is in this township, three things drive a fast sale: the township's resale certificate, the state's seller fees, and the Gloucester County assessment calendar. An owner can hire an agent, sell without one, or sign with a cash buyer who accepts the house as-is, and the same steps apply to all three.

The township covers 21.35 square miles of land in northern Gloucester County and borders Deptford, Mantua, Monroe, Glassboro, Pitman and Gloucester Township. Owners occupy 83.1% of homes. The median owner-occupied value is $337,600, monthly owner costs run $2,437 with a mortgage and $1,153 without, and median household income is $114,249. The township counts 18,444 households.

That median value sits just under $350,000, the line where the state Realty Transfer Fee schedule changes. A sale at or below that price uses a lower rate table than a sale above it, so the contract price decides which table applies. Ask your closing attorney to run both numbers before you accept an offer.

Two centers anchor local business. One is the town center around Greentree Road, Egg Harbor Road, Ganttown Road and Hurffville-Crosskeys Road, near Washington Lake Park. The other follows Route 42, which links Philadelphia to the Jersey Shore.

Route 42 (Black Horse Pike) runs along the east side, Route 47 (Delsea Drive) along the west, and the Atlantic City Expressway ends at Route 42 inside the township. Route 55 clips the eastern tip, and county roads 534 and 555 feed local traffic. Of the 199.78 miles of public road, 154.61 miles belong to the township, so most streets are maintained by the municipality.

  • PATCO Speedline and the NJ Transit Atlantic City line are at Lindenwold, about 10 miles northeast.
  • NJ Transit buses 315, 400, 403, 408 and 412 run to Philadelphia, and route 463 serves local stops.

The Housing office at the municipal building, 523 Egg Harbor Road in Sewell, runs certificate of occupancy inspections so buyers and tenants move into a safe property. The township offers a Certificate of Resale Application and an inspection checklist. The office phone is 856-589-0520.

Get the current application, fee and inspection timing from that office before you sign a contract, and have repairs finished before the inspector arrives. A failed item can delay settlement, so fix the obvious ones, such as smoke alarms, handrails and missing permits, before the inspector comes.

  • State rules call for sealed ten-year smoke alarms in one- and two-family houses before they change hands.
  • For rentals, the township requires proof of liability insurance and a passed lead-based paint inspection certification on units built before 1978.
  • Landlords with tenants in place should ask the Housing office about landlord registration before they sell.

If the property relies on a well or septic system, the Housing office can point you to Gloucester County's well and septic information. The county also keeps online deed records, where you can confirm how your deed reads before the sale.

Bring the address, the block and lot from your tax bill, and a note of any work done since you bought. Ask staff to confirm whether a closed permit is on file for each item. A cash buyer may accept a house with some open items, but the inspector will not, so settle in writing who pays to close them.

For a price at or under $350,000 the state chart starts at $2.00 per $500 and rises to $3.90 for the $200,000 to $350,000 slice. Seniors, blind or disabled sellers and certain income-restricted housing use a separate reduced chart that begins at $0.50 per $500.

Each owner also signs a GIT/REP form for the deed. A resident who stays in the state files GIT/REP-3 and prepays nothing, but a seller leaving New Jersey may prepay income tax at closing. Your title company can match the form to each owner.

Gloucester County is on the alternative assessment calendar, so the deadline to appeal is January 15. File Form A-1 with the Gloucester County Board of Taxation, 1200 North Delsea Drive, Clayton, or call 856-307-6445. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 can file with the Tax Court.

The township's tax office takes payments online through the township site. Pay any open balance before closing so the title search comes back clean.

Keep both numbers handy once you have a contract. Between them they control the two dates a buyer will ask about: when the house can pass inspection and whether any appeal is pending on the assessment.

• Agent listing: more showings and the widest buyer pool, with mortgage approval and appraisal timelines.
  • Private sale: no commission, but you handle contracts, disclosures and township paperwork.
  • Cash offer: no lender, no appraisal contingency, and a buyer willing to take on repairs and the resale certificate.

Before choosing a route, add up what you owe at closing: the mortgage payoff, any unpaid township tax, the transfer fee and any repair credit a buyer requests. Weigh what each route nets you after those items, and get a buyer's proof of funds and closing date in writing.

Start with the certificate, because the inspection is the part of a Washington Township sale you control least. Call the Housing office, ask for the current application and fee, and find out how far ahead you need to book. Fix smoke alarms, handrails and any unpermitted work while you wait for a date.

Next, settle your price against the $350,000 line, since it changes which fee table applies. Then gather documents for the closing attorney: the deed, your mortgage payoff request, a tax payment record and the signed GIT/REP forms for every owner. If the house has tenants, bring the lease and ask the Housing office about landlord registration.

A cash buyer can often close in a few weeks because there is no lender to wait on, but the township inspection still sets the earliest date.

faqs.q: How quickly could a Washington Township sale close?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close in a few weeks, while a listed sale runs longer because of showings, the buyer's loan and the township resale inspection. Call the Housing office at 856-589-0520 to book the inspection early.

faqs.q: Is this the Gloucester County Washington Township?
faqs.a: Yes, it covers the township that includes Sewell, Turnersville and Grenloch. New Jersey has five townships named Washington, so check the county on your tax bill.

faqs.q: What is the cutoff for a Washington Township assessment appeal?
faqs.a: January 15, because Gloucester County uses the alternative calendar. File with the Gloucester County Board of Taxation in Clayton, or call 856-307-6445 for forms.

faqs.q: Why does a $350,000 price matter on a Washington Township sale?
faqs.a: The state's transfer fee chart has one table for prices up to $350,000 and a higher one above it. The median home value here is $337,600, so many sales sit near that line.
Route 42, Route 47, Route 168 and the Atlantic City Expressway cross it, and Route 55 clips the eastern tip. Lindenwold, about 10 miles away, has PATCO and NJ Transit rail.
